intro: Today's material is a coherent set: two agentic-AI primers on how to build and secure agents responsibly, paired with two banking examples showing what that discipline looks like in practice — a bank that kept humans in the loop and a modernization approach that has to precede any of it.

cards.title: A Practical Guide to Building Agents
cards.bite: Start with a single agent, and only split into multiple agents when you hit concrete failure signals — too many overlapping tools (roughly 15+) or branching logic that's become unmanageable — not because multi-agent sounds more impressive. Guardrails should be layered: input filtering, limits on what tools an agent can invoke, and a human checkpoint for consequential actions, because no single safeguard is enough on its own.
cards.read_if: Read if you advise customers on agent architecture decisions; skip if you only need the security angle.
cards.key_takeaway: Start with a single agent and only split into multiple agents when you hit concrete failure signals — like tool overload (more than ~15 overlapping tools) or unmanageable branching logic — not because multi-agent sounds more sophisticated; and guardrails should be layered (input filtering, tool-use limits, human-in-the-loop) because no single guardrail is sufficient on its own.

cards.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
cards.source: arXiv (Yao, Shinn, Razavi, Narasimhan / Sierra Research & Princeton)
cards.bite: This benchmark tests agents on realistic multi-turn tasks involving tools and a simulated user, and even top function-calling agents succeeded on fewer than half of them. Its key metric, pass^k, measures success across repeated attempts rather than a single run, and shows reliability drops off sharply the more times you retry — meaning an agent that works in a live demo tells you almost nothing about whether it will work consistently in production.
cards.read_if: Read if you need to sanity-check vendor benchmark claims; skip if you're not evaluating agent reliability numbers directly.
cards.key_takeaway: Even state-of-the-art function-calling agents were shown to succeed on fewer than half of realistic multi-turn tasks, and the paper's pass^k metric revealed that reliability across repeated attempts is far worse than single-run success rate — meaning a demo that works once tells you almost nothing about production reliability.

cards.title: The lethal trifecta for AI agents: private data, untrusted content, and external communication
cards.bite: An AI agent becomes genuinely dangerous only when three things are true at once: it has access to private data, it's exposed to untrusted content, and it has a way to send information out. Remove any one leg and the exploit path disappears — which is why the robust fix is architectural (never let one execution path have all three) rather than trusting an instruction telling the agent to behave safely.
cards.read_if: Read if you discuss agent permissioning or security architecture with customers; skip if you only care about capability, not risk.
cards.key_takeaway: An agent only becomes dangerously exploitable when it simultaneously has all three of: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and a way to communicate externally — so the most robust defense is architectural (remove one leg of the trifecta from any given execution path) rather than relying on prompt-level instructions to behave safely.

cards.title: Lloyds Banking Group deploys agentic AI to strengthen real-time fraud protection
cards.bite: A major UK retail bank built its fraud-detection agent in-house, running multiple agents in parallel behind the tools its frontline staff already use. Crucially, the bank kept humans as the accountable decision-makers rather than letting the agents make fraud calls autonomously — a deliberate design choice, not a limitation of the technology.
cards.read_if: Read if you're selling into UK or European retail banks on fraud or agentic use cases; skip if you need vendor-neutral technical depth.
cards.key_takeaway: Lloyds built its fraud agent in-house on its own secure AI platform ("Envoy") with multiple agents running in parallel behind frontline colleague tools, explicitly keeping humans as the accountable decision-makers rather than automating the fraud decision itself.

cards.title: Modernizing Core Banking Systems: A Strategic Guide for Financial Leaders
cards.bite: Batch-oriented mainframe cores can't feed the real-time, event-driven data that agentic AI needs, which is the real reason many bank AI projects stall before they start. What's changed is that AI can now do the reverse-engineering step — extracting business logic and dependency maps from decades-old COBOL — that used to take months, and new services can run alongside the mainframe during transition instead of requiring a full replacement.
cards.read_if: Read if you talk to a bank's infrastructure or core-modernization team; skip if your conversations stay at the business-use-case level.
cards.key_takeaway: AI has changed the modernization cost equation by automating the reverse-engineering step — extracting business logic and dependency maps from COBOL/mainframe code that used to take months of manual work — while letting new microservices run alongside the mainframe during transition instead of requiring a rip-and-replace.
